book: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology, 4th ed. (Rizzo)
kicker: Lesson 4 of your course, built from Chapter 4 of your Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Rizzo). Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: Metabolism: building up and breaking down
teach: Metabolism is all the chemical changes inside a cell. Anabolism uses energy to build large molecules from small ones. Catabolism breaks large molecules into small ones and releases energy.

Cells break down (catabolize) carbohydrates, fats and proteins step by step, and use the released energy (measured in calories) to make ATP from ADP and phosphate. ATP is the energy every cell process runs on.
All of this food energy starts with photosynthesis in plants, which turns light energy into glucose.

mnemonic.explanation: Anabolic reactions build up and cost energy; catabolic reactions break down and release it.

steps.title: Cellular respiration: the big picture
teach: Cellular (biochemical) respiration is the oxygen-requiring, or aerobic, way cells make ATP. It isn’t the same as breathing. Overall: glucose + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + ATP.

Glucose is the most common substance broken down aerobically to make ATP. The process is continuous, but it’s taught in three steps: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, then the Krebs citric acid cycle and the electron transport system in the mitochondria.

items.label: Glycolysis
items.detail: Cytoplasm. Doesn’t need oxygen. Glucose → 2 pyruvic acid.

items.label: Krebs citric acid cycle
items.detail: Mitochondria. Needs oxygen. Releases CO₂, loads NAD and FAD.

items.label: Electron transport system
items.detail: Mitochondrial cristae. Needs oxygen. Makes most of the ATP.

items.label: Electron transport
items.feedback: On the cristae of the mitochondria.

steps.title: Glycolysis
teach: Glycolysis is the first step for both aerobic and anaerobic breakdown of glucose. Because it doesn’t need oxygen, it’s sometimes called anaerobic respiration.

It costs 2 ATP to start (adding phosphates to glucose, called phosphorylation). The six-carbon sugar splits into two three-carbon PGAL molecules, which become PGA and then two pyruvic acid molecules, making 4 ATP. Net gain: 2 ATP.
Two NADH₂ are also made. If oxygen is present, they send their electrons through electron transport for 6 more ATP, so aerobic glycolysis gives 8 ATP in total. Anaerobic glycolysis gives only 2.

act.prompt: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP to start and produces 4 ATP. What is the net gain?
act.explanation: 4 made minus the 2 paid back = 2 ATP. With oxygen, the 2 NADH₂ add 6 more, for 8.

steps.title: The Krebs citric acid cycle
teach: With oxygen present, each pyruvic acid enters the mitochondria. In a transition step it loses a carbon as CO₂ and becomes acetyl-CoA. Hans Krebs described the cycle in 1937.

Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetic acid to make citric acid (the cycle’s name). Citric acid is broken down step by step (alpha-ketoglutaric acid, succinic acid, malic acid) back to oxaloacetic acid, releasing CO₂ and passing hydrogens to the carriers NAD and FAD.
Per pyruvic acid: 3 CO₂, 4 NADH₂, 1 FADH₂ and 1 ATP (as GTP). Each glucose makes two pyruvic acids, so double everything.

act.prompt: Where does the Krebs citric acid cycle take place?

options.label: In the mitochondria
options.feedback: Right, on the cristae and in the matrix.

options.label: In the nucleus
options.feedback: The nucleus holds DNA. Respiration happens in the mitochondria.

steps.title: Electron transport and the ATP total
teach: Most ATP is made in the electron transport system on the mitochondrial cristae. NAD and FAD hand on the electrons they collected. As electrons pass from carrier to carrier (NAD, FAD, quinone, cytochromes), they give up energy that’s used to make ATP.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. It takes the electrons and hydrogens and forms water. That’s why breaking down glucose needs oxygen.
Each NADH₂ yields 3 ATP and each FADH₂ yields 2. The textbook totals 38 ATP per glucose (or 36 ATP plus 2 GTP), capturing about 60% of glucose’s energy.
steps.goodToKnow: Newer textbooks often give a lower total, about 30 to 32 ATP. For your course test, use the textbook’s 38.

act.prompt: What is the final electron acceptor in electron transport?

options.label: Oxygen
options.feedback: Right. Oxygen takes the electrons and forms water.

options.label: NAD
options.feedback: NAD is a carrier that passes electrons on.

options.label: Carbon dioxide
options.feedback: CO₂ is a waste product of the Krebs cycle.

steps.title: Without oxygen: fermentation and lactic acid
teach: Glucose can be broken down without oxygen in two situations. Both start with glycolysis and make only 2 ATP per glucose.
Fermentation happens in yeast. Pyruvic acid becomes CO₂ and acetaldehyde, which becomes ethyl alcohol. The CO₂ makes bread rise; the alcohol is used in beer and wine.

In human muscle, when exercise outpaces the oxygen supply, NADH₂ passes its hydrogens to pyruvic acid, forming lactic acid. Lactic acid builds up and causes short-term muscle fatigue. When oxygen returns, it’s converted back to pyruvic acid. The textbook calls this anaerobic respiration.

act.prompt: Fermentation (yeast) or anaerobic respiration in muscle?

items.label: Makes bread rise
items.feedback: The CO₂ from yeast does this.

steps.title: Other foods in the "cellular furnace"
teach: We don’t only eat glucose. Other foods join respiration at the step that matches their structure.

Glucose is a simple carbohydrate. Starch, glycogen and other sugars enter where glucose does. Digestion breaks fat into fatty acids and glycerol: glycerol enters glycolysis at the PGA stage, and fatty acids enter the Krebs cycle. Proteins become amino acids, which enter at pyruvic acid or at different points in the Krebs cycle.

act.prompt: Where does each food piece enter?

items.label: Glutamic acid (amino acid)
items.feedback: Resembles alpha-ketoglutaric acid in the cycle.

steps.title: Discovering DNA
teach: Friedrich Miescher found DNA in 1869 and called it nuclein. In the 1920s P. A. Levine showed it contained phosphate, a five-carbon sugar and nitrogen bases.

In 1953 Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray photograph showed DNA was a helix. James Watson and Francis Crick used it to work out the full 3D structure and won the Nobel Prize in 1962 (with Maurice Wilkins). Franklin had died of cancer before then. Today all three are credited.

act.prompt: Whose X-ray work showed that DNA is a helix?

options.label: Hans Krebs
options.feedback: Krebs described the citric acid cycle.

steps.title: DNA structure and replication
teach: DNA is the hereditary material of the cell. It controls which proteins are made, and so controls the cell’s chemistry.

It’s a double helix of nucleotides, like a spiral staircase: the handrails are sugar and phosphate, and the steps are base pairs. Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds); guanine pairs with cytosine (three). A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.
A gene is a sequence of base pairs that codes for a protein. The Human Genome Project found about 3 billion base pairs coding over 30,000 genes (the textbook’s figures).
Before a cell divides, DNA replicates: helicase enzymes unzip the hydrogen bonds, and DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides to each strand.

act.prompt: Which base pairs with each one in DNA?

steps.title: The cell cycle and interphase
teach: Cellular reproduction is how a single cell duplicates itself. The cell cycle has three main stages: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis.

Interphase is the longest stage. It isn’t division, but the cell is very busy. The DNA is unwound and visible only as threads of chromatin. G1 is the main growth phase. In the S (synthesis) phase, DNA duplicates, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. In G2 the cell gets ready: centrioles start to separate, mitochondria replicate and tubulin is made.
Speed varies: embryo cells cycle in under 20 minutes, a typical mammal cell in about 24 hours. Liver cells divide only if damaged; nerve and muscle cells rarely divide.

act.prompt: Put the phases of interphase in order.

steps.title: Mitosis
teach: Mitosis divides the nucleus into two identical nuclei. The daughter cells are exact copies (clones) of the parent cell.

Prophase: chromosomes shorten and thicken and become visible as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Centrioles move to opposite poles and spindle fibers form. The nuclear membrane breaks down.

Metaphase: chromosomes line up on the equatorial (metaphase) plate. Anaphase, the shortest stage: centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles in a V shape. Telophase: chromosomes uncoil, the spindle breaks down and a nuclear membrane forms around each set.

mnemonic.explanation: Metaphase = Middle, Anaphase = Apart, Telophase = Two nuclei.

act.prompt: Put the stages of mitosis in order.

items.label: Prophase
items.detail: Chromosomes appear; spindle forms; nuclear membrane breaks down

items.label: Metaphase
items.detail: Chromosomes line up at the middle

steps.title: Cytokinesis
teach: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to finish making two cells. It can start in anaphase.

In animal cells, a ring of actin filaments pinches the membrane inward, forming a cleavage furrow until the cell splits. Plant cells build a cell plate across the middle instead, which becomes a new cell wall.

act.prompt: In animal cells, the pinching-in of the membrane during cytokinesis is called a:

options.label: Metaphase plate
options.feedback: That’s where chromosomes line up in metaphase.

steps.title: Meiosis
teach: Sexual reproduction joins two gametes (sperm and egg) into a fertilized egg, or zygote, giving offspring more genetic variety. Gametes are made by meiosis, which happens only in the gonads (ovaries and testes).
Meiosis is a reduction division: body cells are diploid (2n, 46 chromosomes), and gametes are haploid (n, 23). Fertilization restores 46.

DNA duplicates once, but there are two divisions. In prophase I, matching (homologous) chromosomes pair up in synapsis, forming tetrads, and may swap segments: crossing-over, seen as an X-shaped chiasma. Meiosis I separates the pairs (46 to 23); meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. The result is four haploid cells.

items.label: Four cells, each with half the chromosomes
Crossing-over can happen
items.feedback: Only in prophase I of meiosis.

steps.title: Making sperm and eggs
teach: The four cells from meiosis still have to mature. This is gametogenesis.

Spermatogenesis happens in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. All four cells become sperm: the nucleus becomes the head, mitochondria gather in the middle piece to power the tail, and the cytoplasm becomes the flagellum. It begins at puberty and continues into old age.

Oogenesis, the formation of the egg, happens in the ovary. The cytoplasm divides unequally, so only one functional egg forms. The smaller cells are polar bodies, which die. Meiosis begins in the female embryo, and egg production stops after menopause.

act.prompt: The first meiotic division of oogenesis makes one large cell and one small cell. The small cell is a:

options.label: Polar body
options.feedback: Right. Polar bodies give their cytoplasm to the egg and then die.

options.label: Sperm
options.feedback: Sperm come from spermatogenesis in the testes.

options.label: Zygote
options.feedback: A zygote is a fertilized egg.

steps.title: When cell division goes wrong
teach: A mutation is a mistake in copying DNA, which can be caused by chemicals (smoke, asbestos), radiation, X-rays or some viruses. If it affects the genes that control division, cells keep dividing and form a tumor. Cells that spread and form tumors elsewhere are metastases.
Carcinomas come from epithelial tissue; sarcomas from connective tissue such as bone. Cancer-causing agents are carcinogens.

Chromosome and gene disorders in the chapter: Down syndrome is usually caused by an extra chromosome 21. Klinefelter’s syndrome affects males with extra X chromosomes, most often XXY. Tay-Sachs disease is an inherited recessive disorder of lipid metabolism. Progeria causes premature aging.

act.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

items.label: A tumor from connective tissue, like bone
A tumor that has spread to a new site

steps.title: Aging and metabolism
teach: With age, metabolism slows because less energy is needed for growth and maintenance, so calorie needs drop. Eating less and exercising daily help prevent the weight gain common from the early 40s.
Women stop producing eggs after menopause, but men keep producing sperm into their 80s.

act.prompt: Why do calorie needs fall with age, according to the textbook?

options.label: Metabolism slows because less energy is needed for growth and maintenance
Cells stop making ATP
options.feedback: Cells always need ATP; they just need less overall.

options.label: Mitochondria disappear
options.feedback: That isn’t what the textbook says.

quiz.q: The most common substance decomposed aerobically in cells to produce ATP is _________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the most common substance decomposed aerobically in cells to produce ATP is glucose. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: What is the net gain of ATP molecules produced by glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport system for each glucose molecule?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook totals 38 ATP per glucose (or 36 ATP and 2 GTP) from glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and electron transport. Newer sources often say about 30 to 32, but this test follows the textbook. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The first step in the anaerobic breakdown of glucose into carbon dioxide gas and water is known as __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the first step in breaking glucose down to carbon dioxide and water is glycolysis, which doesn’t need oxygen. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Which term refers to the breakdown of glucose in human muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient due to muscle fatigue?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 calls the breakdown of glucose in muscle cells without enough oxygen anaerobic respiration. Fermentation is the yeast version. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.
Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says glucose is a simple carbohydrate. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Males who have an extra X chromosome (47,XXY) have __________________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says Klinefelter’s syndrome is caused by extra X chromosomes in males, most commonly XXY. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Biochemical respiration is the oxygen-requiring or process of ATP production.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says biochemical respiration is strictly the oxygen-requiring, or aerobic, process of ATP production. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Sister chromatids are attached to one another at the __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says sister chromatids are attached to each other at the centromere. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: When we cut a finger, cells are repaired and replaced by __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says that when we cut a finger, the cells are repaired and replaced by mitosis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Cancer-causing agents are called __________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says cancer-causing agents are called carcinogens. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The first meiotic division of oogenesis yields one large cell and one smaller cell called a(n) __________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says unequal division in oogenesis makes smaller cells called polar bodies. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The Krebs citric acid cycle takes place in the __________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the Krebs citric acid cycle takes place in the mitochondria. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Most of the ATP produced during biochemical respiration is produced in the ______________________ system.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says most of the ATP made during biochemical respiration is produced in the electron transport system. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate electron acceptor for the electrons captured by the cofactors during glucose decomposition?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says oxygen is the ultimate electron acceptor for the electrons captured by the cofactors. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Digestion decomposes fat molecules into fatty acids and __________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says digestion decomposes fat into fatty acids and glycerol. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Development of eggs in females is called __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the formation of the female egg is called oogenesis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Unwound strands of chromosomes visible as threads in the nucleoplasm are called _______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the unwound strands of chromosomes are visible only as dark threads called chromatin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The indentation of the cell membrane during cytokinesis is called a __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says animal cells separate by a pinching-in of the membrane called a cleavage furrow. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The process by which a single cell duplicates itself is known as __________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says cellular reproduction is the process by which a single cell duplicates itself. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: What is the hereditary material of the cell?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says DNA is the hereditary material of the cell. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Which term refers to a fertilized egg?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the sperm and egg unite to form a fertilized egg, or zygote. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The special kind of cellular reproduction that occurs only in gametes is known as mitosis.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The special division that makes gametes is meiosis, not mitosis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The formation of the female egg is called oogenesis.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says the formation of the female egg is called oogenesis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Down syndrome is a congenital defect commonly caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says Down syndrome is a congenital defect commonly caused by an extra chromosome 21. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Fermentation in yeast cells is a type of aerobic respiration.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Fermentation in yeast is anaerobic: it happens without oxygen. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 4.
